Apple may surprise the tech world by unveiling an iPad 3 later this fall, despite the iPad 2 having only recently launched. According to rumors, the new iPad would come as a surprise, given Apple's typical product development cycles. The "fall surprise" is linked to the iPad 3, suggesting a new iteration of the tablet could be released in the coming months. While Apple hasn't officially acknowledged the iPad 2, leaks and reports from sources indicate the iPad 3 could feature a higher-resolution screen, a faster processor, and support for 4G networks. Apple's history of not resting on its laurels and continuously improving its products suggests the company might indeed release an iPad 3 to maintain its competitive edge. However, details about the iPad 3's features and release date remain speculative, and Apple could still adjust its plans.

On the heels of World AIDS Day, doctors announced that an HIV-positive man, known as the "Berlin Patient," has been cured of HIV following a stem cell transplant. This breakthrough, detailed in a report published in the journal Blood, suggests a path for a permanent cure through genetically engineered stem cells. The patient, Timothy Ray Brown, received the transplant in 2007 as part of a treatment course for leukemia. Extensive testing "strongly suggests" the virus has been eradicated, with no detectable HIV by viral load testing or tests for viral DNA within cells. This case, while not a definitive cure, offers hope for the millions living with HIV worldwide and highlights advancements in HIV treatment and prevention strategies.

Charlie Sheen and Warner Bros. have settled their dispute over "Two and a Half Men." A rep for Warner Bros. stated, "Warner Bros. Television, Chuck Lorre, and Charlie Sheen have resolved their dispute to the parties’ mutual satisfaction." According to TMZ, Sheen will receive around $100 million in profits from the syndication of the show over the next 7 years. Both parties have agreed to dismiss their mutual lawsuit against each other.

Democrats face a critical decision following Scott Brown's victory in the Massachusetts Senate race, as health care reform appears to be in jeopardy. Publicly, the White House and Speaker Nancy Pelosi maintain their stance that health care reform will pass this year, but privately, Democrats are reconsidering their strategy. Options to salvage the bill include passing the Senate bill through the House and Senate before Brown is seated, or using a two-step process where the House adopts the Senate bill and then makes additional changes through reconciliation. However, both options have significant drawbacks and may not be palatable to all House Democrats. A Brown win could force Democrats to recalibrate their approach and convince a skeptical caucus that this is the only viable path forward.

A destructive rodent known as the nutria has been spotted in Stanislaus County, prompting a multi-agency task force to address the potential threat. The nutria, native to South America and capable of consuming large amounts of vegetation and damaging infrastructure, has been sighted in Fresno, Merced, and Stanislaus counties. Officials are concerned about the potential impact on agriculture, wetlands, and levees. Nutria can give birth to up to 200 offspring annually, making quick eradication crucial. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife has set traps and cameras to monitor the situation and is urging the public to report any sightings.

Parents in the United States report significantly lower happiness levels compared to non-parents, a phenomenon known as the "parenting happiness gap." However, new research from the Council on Contemporary Families reveals that this gap varies across 22 countries, with some nations showing no gap or even a happiness surplus for parents. The study, led by Jennifer Glass, University of Texas, Robin Simon, Wake Forest University, and Matthew Andersson, Baylor University, analyzed data from surveys conducted prior to the global recession, focusing on social policies that support working parents. These policies include paid leave, sick and vacation days, and affordable child care. The research found that countries with comprehensive family-friendly policies eliminate the happiness gap, often by enhancing the overall happiness of both parents and non-parents. The study suggests that policies that help parents also benefit the broader community, making it clear that investing in working parents can lead to a happier society.

A 17-year-old student at Millard South High School in Omaha, Nebraska, opened fire on Wednesday, fatally wounding the assistant principal and forcing students to take cover in the kitchen. The shooter, Robert Butler Jr., had attended the school for no more than two months before the incident. He also wounded the principal before fleeing and fatally shooting himself in his car about a mile away. In a Facebook post, Butler expressed unhappiness with his new school and apologized for the lives he ruined. He had transferred from a high school in Lincoln, about 50 miles southwest of Omaha. Friends described Butler as energetic and outgoing, but authorities are interviewing his father, a detective for the Omaha Police Department, to understand his motivations. The assistant principal, Vicki Kaspar, died at a hospital, while the principal, Curtis Case, was in stable condition. Students were released in groups after the lockdown, and parents applauded when the first group emerged.

This weekend, the Leonid meteor shower will put on a show, with up to 60 meteors per hour expected to streak across the sky late Saturday night and into Sunday morning. The best viewing time is after the moon sets but before dawn, with NASA recommending finding a dark spot away from city lights and allowing 30 minutes for your eyes to adjust to the darkness. The meteors appear to come from the constellation Leo, but it's better to look away from this point for longer, more spectacular meteors. These meteors come from the comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a debris trail as it orbits the sun. While the 1966 storm was impressive, with thousands of meteors per hour, recent years have seen weaker displays. Still, the 2034 display might be worth watching, with potential rates in the hundreds per hour. Bundle up and get cozy for the best experience.

An unarmed security guard at Las Vegas' Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino, Jesus Campos, was the first to confront gunman Stephen Paddock, getting shot in the process but providing crucial assistance to police. Campos, identified by the International Union, Security, Police and Fire Professionals of America, was shot in the leg after Paddock fired at him through a door. He managed to direct police to Paddock's suite and even provided a hotel key to officers clearing rooms. Campos, praised as a "remarkable man" by the Clark County Sheriff, engaged Paddock, who fired over 200 rounds into the hallway. Campos continued clearing rooms until ordered to seek medical attention. His actions were crucial in stopping the shooting, which killed 58 and injured hundreds.

Parents of some of the Sandy Hook victims plan to sue Bushmaster, the manufacturer of the AR-15 rifle used in the 2012 shooting, according to reports. The lawsuit, filed by a law firm that previously represented Michael Jackson’s family, aims to argue that the sale of the AR-15 to an individual deemed unfit to possess it contributed to the tragedy. The parents have opened estates in their children’s names to sue on their behalf, citing the weapon’s design as enabling the rapid and efficient killing of 26 people in just five minutes. The case highlights ongoing debates over gun control and the role of manufacturers in preventing mass shootings.

A South Carolina woman who died during a medical emergency on an American Airlines flight from Hawaii to Dallas is the subject of a wrongful death lawsuit filed by her family. Brittany Oswell, 25, began experiencing symptoms mid-flight, including dizziness and disorientation, and eventually went into cardiac arrest. A doctor on board asked the crew to land the plane for medical care, but the flight continued to Dallas. Upon landing, Oswell was taken to a hospital where she was diagnosed with an embolism and brain damage. Despite efforts by medical personnel, she was declared brain dead and removed from life support. The lawsuit alleges negligence by the airline, including faulty medical equipment and failure to divert the flight. The family seeks damages for emotional distress and loss.

Sharbat Gula, known as the "Afghan Girl" from a famous 1984 National Geographic photograph, was arrested in Pakistan on charges of possessing a forged national identification card, according to authorities. She could face up to 14 years in prison. The incident highlights ongoing issues with fake IDs and refugee status in Pakistan, where over a million Afghans have sought refuge. Gula's story, which became a symbol of the refugee plight, has spanned decades, from her childhood in a Nasir Bagh refugee camp to her recent arrest. Her case underscores the challenges faced by refugees in maintaining valid documents in a country grappling with security and identity verification.

Taylor Swift filed a counter suit against David Mueller, a radio host who allegedly groped her during a meet-and-greet in 2013. Mueller had previously sued Swift, claiming he was fired and banned from her concerts based on false allegations of a prior incident. In her countersuit, Swift alleges Mueller intentionally groped her during a meet-and-greet, stating he lifted her skirt and touched an intimate part of her body. Swift was reportedly surprised, upset, and alarmed by the incident and informed her photographer, tour manager, and security team. She demands a jury trial and plans to donate any winnings to organizations protecting women from sexual assault.

Kristen Wiig, who left Saturday Night Live (SNL) after last season, is set to return as host on May 11th, with Vampire Weekend as musical guests. This marks her first hosting gig since a seven-year run on the show. Wiig's departure was marked by an emotional sendoff, but her return is expected to bring back some of her most memorable characters and sketches, such as "Two A-holes," "Rebecca Larue," and "Kathy Lee and Elisabeth Hasselbeck." Fans are eager to see her reprise roles like Penelope and Judy Grimes, as well as any new material she might bring. The show will also feature Zach Galifianakis hosting on May 4th, with Of Monsters and Men as musical guests. Argo director and star Ben Affleck will close out the 38th season on May 18th, hosting for the fifth time with Kanye West as musical guest.

The Thomas fire, the largest wildfire in recorded California history, has been officially declared extinguished after burning more than 440 square miles and destroying over 1,000 buildings in Ventura and Santa Barbara counties. The blaze, ignited by Santa Ana winds in December 2017, led to two deaths, including a state firefighter. A massive downpour triggered deadly mudslides, causing 21 deaths and extensive damage in Montecito. The fire's aftermath saw numerous lawsuits against Southern California Edison, though the utility maintains the cause remains under investigation. Efforts are underway to repair trails and damaged infrastructure in the affected areas.

A new startup called Ouya is aiming to disrupt the living room console market with an open Android-based gaming device priced at just $99. The company, led by Julie Uhrman, is launching a Kickstarter campaign to raise funds, with the potential for developers to create and experiment with games for the platform. Ouya encourages openness, allowing developers to add hardware and modify the console. The device features a quad-core CPU, 8GB of flash memory, and a touchpad for enhanced gaming experiences. Ouya promises free games with monetization through virtual goods or subscriptions, and it aims to democratize game development by providing tools and a low-cost platform. The goal is to bring back innovation and creativity to console gaming, making it more accessible and affordable for developers and gamers alike.

Neil Armstrong, the first man to walk on the moon, has died at the age of 82. He commanded the Apollo 11 mission, landing on the moon on July 20, 1969, and famously said, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." Armstrong was a quiet, unassuming engineer who preferred to focus on the team that helped him achieve his historic feat rather than his own accomplishments. After leaving NASA, he taught aerospace engineering at the University of Cincinnati and remained mostly out of the public eye. Armstrong's family asked people to honor his modesty and modest accomplishments, suggesting that the next time they see the moon, they should give him a wink. His death was mourned by many public figures, including President Barack Obama, who praised Armstrong as one of the greatest American heroes.

A report from the Pew Center on the States indicates that over 24 million voter registration records in the U.S. are inaccurate, out-of-date, or duplicates, affecting about one in eight registered voters. Nearly 2.8 million people are registered in two or more states, and perhaps 1.8 million registered voters are deceased. Experts argue that while these errors do not lead to Election Day fraud, they result in wasted resources. The 1993 National Voter Registration Act, known as the "motor voter" law, made voter registration easier but also made it harder to remove ineligible voters. Swing states face particular challenges due to frequent voter registration activities that can result in inaccurate records. Ohio Secretary of State Jon Husted is seeking guidance from the U.S. Justice Department on how to clean up voter rolls without violating the motor voter law. Scientists have discovered that bottlenose dolphins can remember each other's signature contact whistles—functioning as names—for over 20 years, the longest social memory recorded in a nonhuman animal. A 5-year study by Jason Bruck, a cognitive ethologist at the University of Chicago, found that dolphins respond more strongly to whistles of former companions they haven't heard in decades compared to unfamiliar calls. This ability is crucial for navigating their complex social lives, as dolphins frequently change groups. The research, published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B, suggests dolphins have cognitive sophistication comparable to humans, chimpanzees, and elephants.

The "presidential alert" to be sent to Americans' cell phones on Wednesday is the first nationwide test of a system designed to push emergency messages to nearly all cell phones in the U.S. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) will send the alert, which will bear the headline "Presidential Alert," and phones will make a loud tone and have a special vibration. The test message will read: “THIS IS A TEST of the National Wireless Emergency Alert System. No action is needed.” A separate alert on TV and radios will be issued at 2:20 p.m. The test aims to ensure that the alert system would work in the event of a national emergency. Government officials emphasized that the president will not personally trigger the alert and that no president could "wake up one morning and attempt to send a personal message." A new study from the University of Kansas School of Medicine suggests that inheriting Alzheimer’s disease from a mother may be more detrimental than from a father. Among 21 adult children (aged 63 to 83) of Alzheimer’s patients who remained cognitively intact, brain scans revealed that those whose mothers had the disease experienced more significant gray matter loss in specific brain regions over a two-year period compared to those whose fathers had the disease or those with no family history. These regions include the left precuneus and left parahippocampal gyrus, which are crucial for memory functions. The researchers noted that the brains of subjects whose fathers had Alzheimer’s were similar to those with no family history, indicating that maternal inheritance may have a stronger impact on brain atrophy. The exact reason for this difference remains unclear, but it could be linked to mitochondrial DNA, which is inherited only from the mother and may affect glucose metabolism in brain tissue affected by Alzheimer’s.

Democratic Rep. Kyrsten Sinema holds a narrow lead over Republican Rep. Martha McSally in Arizona's uncalled Senate race, with Sinema leading by 9,610 votes as of Thursday evening. More than 1.8 million votes have been counted, but about half a million remain to be tallied, mostly from Maricopa County. Both campaigns are confident their candidate will prevail once all votes are counted. The race is expected to continue for several days, with potential legal challenges. Arizona is one of three remaining Senate races without a declared winner, alongside Florida and Mississippi. The outcome could affect the Republican majority in the Senate, with Democrats needing to defend 22 Senate seats in 2020 compared to just 12 for Republicans.

Shadow is a declawed male domestic grey shorthair cat, 12 weeks old at adoption on 9/3/2005. Due to an anaphylactic allergy, his owner had to relinquish him. He is neutered, up to date on vaccinations, and on a special diet. Shadow loves to be close to people, following them and sitting by their feet or laps. He prefers gentle head strokes and avoids being petted near his tail. He adjusts well to children and enjoys lying by the fire. Shadow came to VIPP on 11/11/15.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has issued new guidelines discouraging any screen time for children under two years old, citing potential links to slower language development. The guidelines also warn parents about the negative effects of their own screen-watching habits on their children. Pediatrician Ari Brown, lead author of the guidelines, explains that passive screen media, such as television, videos, and web-streamed content, can reduce parent-child interaction, which is crucial for a child's language development. The guidelines do not include interactive media like video games. The AAP also criticizes the $200 million annual market of baby DVDs, stating that their educational claims are unproven. The guidelines suggest that unstructured playtime is more beneficial for a child's development than screen time.

Kim Kardashian-West revealed at the Vogue Festival in association with Harrods that she is moving away from heavy contouring, opting for a more natural look. She stated that she now travels with a smaller makeup case and prefers strobing over contouring. Kardashian-West, who gave birth to her second child, Saint, without makeup, also shared her current makeup essentials, including a Charlotte Tilbury lipstick, mascara, and a MAC kabuki brush. She credited her mother’s makeup collection and her father’s support for her early makeup education. Despite this shift, Kardashian-West emphasized that wearing makeup makes her feel empowered and confident. The event concluded with a perfect selfie taken by Kardashian-West and makeup artist Charlotte Tilbury.

Diet Coke's "You're on" campaign, introduced three months ago, is being replaced after facing mockery on social media. The ads, which aimed to position Diet Coke as a pick-me-up for young strivers, are being replaced with a more traditional "Just for the taste of it" campaign, which debuted in 1982 and has returned multiple times since. The abrupt end of the "You're on" ads comes after bloggers noticed that the theme could be read as "You're on Diet Coke," potentially evoking drug references. Coca-Cola North America responded that the campaign aimed to celebrate ambitious young achievers and denied any endorsement of illegal substances. The new campaign focuses on the taste and sugar-free status of Diet Coke, aiming to resonate with core loyal followers.

Michelle Williams, 37, has entered a new chapter of her life, both professionally and personally, as she reveals her marriage to indie musician Phil Elverum, 40, for the first time. The couple tied the knot in a secret ceremony in the Adirondacks, with a few friends and their daughters present. Williams, known for her private nature, has long shunned the spotlight but is now thrust into the spotlight due to the gender pay gap in Hollywood and a new superhero movie. She discusses her recent experience of being paid less than 1% of her male co-star's fee for reshoots in the film "All the Money in the World," which sparked a cultural conversation and eventually led to a donation from her co-star, Mark Wahlberg. Williams emphasizes the importance of women supporting each other and advocates for equal pay. She also shares that she has found a new love, describing her relationship with Elverum as "very sacred and very special."

President Donald Trump took steps to advance the Keystone XL and Dakota Access oil pipelines, signing executive orders to expedite their construction. The orders do not grant final permits but aim to move both projects toward approval. Trump emphasized the importance of job creation and energy security, stating that pipelines should use American-made materials. The orders are a significant departure from the Obama administration, which rejected the Keystone proposal in 2015 and blocked Dakota Access. Environmentalists and the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe oppose the Dakota Access project, citing concerns over water safety and cultural sites. The actions signal a shift in the administration’s stance on infrastructure projects, potentially benefiting the oil industry and creating jobs.

Former national security adviser Michael Flynn worked as a paid lobbyist for Turkey while advising then-candidate Trump, according to documents he disclosed to the Trump transition team. Despite this, Trump appointed Flynn as his national security adviser, raising questions about the administration’s handling of potential conflicts of interest. Flynn’s lobbying work involved meetings with Turkish officials and a meeting with the Turkish foreign minister, which occurred after Flynn had been named as Trump’s national security adviser. Flynn’s actions, particularly his decision to delay a military operation against the Islamic State, have raised concerns about his influence and potential vulnerability to Russian blackmail. The revelation of Flynn’s work for Turkey has sparked renewed scrutiny of the Trump administration’s relationship with the country and its handling of potential conflicts of interest.

BP's $20 billion compensation fund for the Gulf oil spill is nearly depleted, with only $300 million left, despite the company's high profits. BP's chief executive, Bob Dudley, suggests that the biggest beneficiaries of the compensation process are plaintiffs' attorneys, who are collecting fees and submitting large claims. Dudley criticizes the U.S. Department of Justice's settlement, which includes a promise not to contest legal fees up to $600 million, arguing that it ensures businesses unharmed by the spill receive compensation. This, he believes, misinterprets the agreement and is not in the best interest of American businesses. Drawing from his experience covering mass litigation, the author reflects on the often questionable motives of plaintiffs' lawyers, who frequently create mass torts to extract billions from corporations. The author argues that the current system unfairly transfers money from BP shareholders to bystanders, questioning the appropriateness of such compensation.

A Navy commander who was accused of having an affair and faking his death to end it has been relieved of his duties as the commanding officer of the USS Pittsburgh, just one week after he took command. The woman, who met the 43-year-old commander through a dating website, said he told her he was separated and that he worked in "special ops." She claimed he got her pregnant, then faked his death in an email in July. The commander, who is married with children, has been reassigned to administrative duties. The Navy stated he was relieved due to a lack of confidence in his ability to command based on allegations of personal misconduct. The woman, who did not want to be identified, said she was hospitalized after learning the commander was alive and had moved to Connecticut. She said she lost the baby due to complications. The commander has not commented on the situation.

Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) is exploring a potential 2016 presidential bid, setting up a committee to test his viability under IRS guidelines. Graham told NBC's "Meet the Press" that he is not polling but is seriously considering the path. Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) has been encouraging Graham to run, seeing him as a potential presidential candidate. Meanwhile, former Arkansas governor Mike Huckabee (R) hinted at a possible run, stating there is a "very strong likelihood" he will declare his intentions later in the spring. Both candidates acknowledge the competitive Republican field and the high risks involved in a presidential campaign.

Cable TV is facing a significant challenge as HBO announces plans to launch a standalone online streaming service in 2015, allowing users to access HBO content without a cable subscription. This move, which follows years of illegal downloads and password sharing, could mark the end of traditional cable television. Critics argue that cable has become an overpriced, monopolistic service offering little choice and poor service. With options like MLB.tv, Netflix, and Hulu already providing a la carte content, the standalone HBO service could further erode cable's market share. However, cable companies are likely to adapt, potentially offering bundled internet and streaming services to retain subscribers. The shift towards online streaming services could lead to a more fragmented and personalized viewing experience, potentially reducing the need for traditional cable packages.

First Lady Michelle Obama inadvertently referred to herself as a "busy single mother" during an interview with CBS affiliate WCAX, highlighting the challenges of balancing a demanding schedule. Correcting herself quickly, she explained, "Sometimes when you’ve got the husband who’s president, it can feel a little single, but he’s there." This slip-up, while brief, underscored the dual roles she navigates as both a high-profile public figure and a working mother.

An unusual genetic disorder, fatal familial insomnia (FFI), has affected multiple generations of the Webbs and Vallabh families, causing a relentless and terrifying insomnia that leads to death. The disorder, first identified in a Venetian family in 1986, is caused by a single gene mutation that can be inherited with a 50% chance. Symptoms typically appear in middle age, with victims experiencing a constant state of wakefulness, hallucinations, and eventually, death. The thalamus, a crucial brain structure, is heavily affected, leading to a breakdown of autonomic functions and sleep. Despite the grim prognosis, family members have turned to scientific research and clinical trials, hoping to find a cure. A vehicle crash in Tiananmen Square, Beijing, has left five people dead and raised concerns about Uighur minority involvement. Police identified the attackers as members of a Muslim minority, including a man, his wife, and his mother. The SUV contained knives, iron rods, gasoline, and a flag with religious slogans. The attack, described as a planned terrorist incident, targeted the political heart of Beijing. Authorities have tightened security in Xinjiang, the Uighur-dominated region, amid fears of further attacks. The incident has heightened tensions and fears of discrimination among Uighurs, who face routine harassment and restrictions on their culture and religion. Uighur activists warn against using the attack to further repress the community and call for a transparent investigation.

On The Bachelor, Arie’s journey to find love took a strange detour. He proposed to Becca and then changed his mind, dumping her and trying to get back with Lauren. The fallout included people Venmo-ing Becca money, a Minnesota state representative promising to draft a bill to ban Arie from the state, and billboards calling Arie a jerk. The After the Final Rose episode showed Becca crying and Arie apologizing. Arie blamed Becca for encouraging him to get closure with Lauren, and The Bachelor producers for feeling pressured to make a decision. Lauren and Arie rekindled their romance, and Arie proposed to her. Becca was confirmed as the next Bachelorette, despite the drama, and expressed readiness to move on and find love.

The West Village brownstone that served as Carrie Bradshaw's home in "Sex and the City" is back on the market for $9.65 million, up from its previous sale price of $9 million. Now asking for $9.65 million, the four-story, 4,100-square-foot home with six fireplaces is attracting new interest, though neighbors are tired of the constant tourist traffic. The house, originally used in early episodes of the show, later switched to the adjacent 66 Perry Street for scenes. Despite its famous address, the brownstone's current listing suggests a shift in its value and appeal, raising questions about the nature of fame and the relationships we form with our environments.

One in four Americans believe the Sun revolves around the Earth, according to a 2012 National Science Foundation survey. The same poll revealed that only 39% correctly stated the universe began with a big bang, and 48% accurately acknowledged that humans evolved from earlier species. Additionally, 55% of young Americans aged 18-24 still consider astrology to be a science. Despite these concerning findings, the survey also showed that the majority of Americans support science research and express interest in medical advancements.

Actor Douglas Rain, known for voicing the iconic HAL 9000 in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey, passed away at 90. HAL's chilling, dry voice became synonymous with the film's suspense and tension. Rain recorded his lines in just 10 hours, with Kubrick providing detailed guidance. The role influenced actors like Anthony Hopkins, who credited HAL for his performance as Hannibal Lecter. Rain also had a long career in theatre, earning a Tony nomination for his work. His unique voice and presence left a lasting impact on science fiction and cinema.

Residents in California's far northern counties, long feeling ignored and out of sync with urban areas, have for over a century considered forming their own state. Voters in Del Norte and Tehama counties will decide June 3 on an advisory measure to join a wider effort to form a 51st state named Jefferson. Supporters argue for better representation and use of natural resources, while opponents warn of economic challenges. Similar efforts to split California into six states or separate Silicon Valley have faced significant hurdles. Despite the long history of such proposals, the path to statehood remains steep, requiring legislative and congressional approval.

Democrats are intensifying their Medicare-saving message in a race for a western New York congressional seat, framing it as a choice between preserving the program and letting Republicans dismantle it. Kathy Hochul, the Democratic candidate, has been successful in selling this narrative, emphasizing that if Republicans have their way, Medicare as seniors know it will end. Her campaign strategy focuses on the Ryan plan's potential to increase prescription drug costs and reduce benefits for future seniors. In contrast, Republican Jane Corwin defends the Ryan plan, arguing that it will save Medicare and protect it for current seniors. However, Corwin faces challenges in convincing voters that she genuinely supports Medicare's preservation, as her attacks on Hochul have been seen as less passionate. The race, entering its final days, highlights the difficulty Republicans face in defending a plan that has become a political liability, especially in a district with a Republican voter advantage.

Hurricane Harvey's aftermath has led to a surge in mosquito populations, raising concerns about the spread of mosquito-borne illnesses in Texas. Public health officials warn that while most of the mosquitoes are nuisance species, some could potentially carry diseases like Zika, dengue, or West Nile. The CDC notes that floodwater mosquitoes hatch in large numbers after major flooding events. Texas has launched aerial spraying of insecticides in affected areas to control the mosquito population and prevent disease outbreaks. Despite the potential for increased mosquito-borne illnesses, experts emphasize that the current mosquito population is primarily nuisance species, and the more dangerous varieties will eventually return. Residents are advised to eliminate standing water, use repellent, and wear protective clothing to minimize exposure.

Republican presidential candidates squared off in New Hampshire, with front-runners Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz facing tough attacks, while governors Jeb Bush, Chris Christie, and John Kasich delivered strong performances. Key moments included Christie's relentless assault on Rubio, accusing him of lacking experience and executive leadership skills. Rubio struggled, repeatedly reverting to scripted responses and facing criticism for his Senate voting record. Donald Trump largely avoided direct challenges, with Jeb Bush and Chris Christie trading blows over issues like eminent domain. Ted Cruz had a mixed night, apologizing for spreading false rumors about Ben Carson and delivering a personal story about his sister's death from drug overdose. The debate highlighted the competition among governors to position themselves for a last-minute surge, with Christie and Bush seeking to undermine Trump and Rubio.

Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh faced new allegations of misconduct during a phone call with Senate Judiciary Committee investigators on Tuesday, according to a transcript released Wednesday. The allegations, which stem from anonymous complaints, describe separate incidents from 1998 and 1985. Kavanaugh denied both accusations, with the 1998 allegation already being recanted. The latest accusations come as pressure mounts on undecided Republican senators to support Kavanaugh, despite growing concerns from Democrats. President Trump expressed willingness to withdraw the nomination if the allegations are true but called them "false." The committee is also investigating claims from attorney Michael Avenatti's client, Julie Swetnick, who alleges witnessing Kavanaugh's involvement in multiple episodes of misconduct. Kavanaugh denied these allegations as well. The Senate Judiciary Committee is scheduled to hold a hearing with Christine Blasey Ford on Thursday, despite the ongoing controversy.

China has announced a ban on all ivory trade and processing activities by the end of 2017, a move that could significantly impact the global ivory market and help curb elephant poaching in Africa. Conservation groups view this as a "game-changer" for elephant conservation, with the United States having already ended its domestic ivory trade earlier this year. The decision follows years of international pressure and a resolution at the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) in October. With China being the world’s largest ivory market, accounting for an estimated 70% of global demand, the ban is expected to send a powerful message and potentially save threatened elephant populations.

A tiger killed a man and wounded another in Tbilisi, Georgia's capital, after escaping from a flooded zoo. The tiger, one of several that broke free due to severe flooding, was shot dead by police. The zoo had previously reported that all dangerous animals had been accounted for, but uncertainty remained about the number of escaped animals, with reports of another tiger being cornered in a city center cafe. The flash floods devastated Tbilisi, claiming 13 lives, including three zookeepers. Up to six people were still missing, and about 40 families lost their homes. Hundreds of volunteers helped clear the mess, digging animals from the mud and carrying them away. Many animals, including lions, hippos, and bears, escaped and were seen roaming the streets, prompting residents to stay indoors.

A controversial Confederate statue known as "Silent Sam" on the University of North Carolina campus in Chapel Hill was toppled by protesters on Monday evening. More than 300 people gathered at the Peace and Justice Plaza before marching to the statue's base. By 9:30 PM, the statue had been brought down using a rope. Tensions between police and protesters led to one arrest. Students, faculty, and alumni have long called for the statue's removal, citing its racist symbolism. The statue, donated by the United Daughters of the Confederacy in 1909 and erected in 1913, was taken to a dump truck by a backhoe after the incident. Governor Roy Cooper condemned the destruction of public property while expressing shared frustration with protesters over the pace of change.

A tapeworm found in fish from Asia has now been discovered in Alaskan salmon, potentially affecting salmon caught along the Pacific coast of North America. The Japanese broad tapeworm, Diphyllobothrium nihonkaiense, was identified in 64 wild pink salmon from Alaska, raising concerns about the safety of raw or undercooked fish. This tapeworm, previously thought to be limited to Asia, can grow up to 30 feet long and may cause symptoms like abdominal discomfort, nausea, and loose stools. While most infections are mild, severe cases can lead to intestinal blockages and inflammation of bile ducts. The CDC advises freezing fish for at least a few days or cooking it to 145°F for four to five minutes to eliminate the tapeworm. Commercial sushi and ceviche are generally safe due to FDA regulations requiring frozen fish. However, consumers who catch or purchase fresh salmon should freeze it before consumption to avoid potential infection.

The Duchess of Cambridge may have inadvertently hinted at the gender of her baby during a recent public appearance. When given a teddy bear, she reportedly said, "Thank you, I’ll take that for my d..." before stopping herself. Well-wishers, including Sandra Cook, believe she was about to say "daughter." Despite the speculation, the royal couple maintains they do not know the gender of their July due date baby, who will one day be the monarch. The Duchess also joked that she might have to wait a long time before she is queen. During her visit to the National Fishing Heritage Centre in Grimsby, she interacted with local dignitaries and patients from a hospice, showing her friendly and down-to-earth side.

Shuttle Atlantis undocked from the International Space Station on Sunday, marking its final voyage. The two craft parted 220 miles above the Indian Ocean, with station astronauts thanking Atlantis for their assistance and urging safe travels. Atlantis is scheduled to land on Wednesday after a final safety inspection. The space station, now 98% complete, has seen significant growth thanks to Atlantis and its crew. Two more shuttle missions will complete NASA's share of construction, with Atlantis potentially making one last trip in June 2011 to deliver supplies. NASA is considering retiring Atlantis to the Smithsonian Institution, while other museums express interest. Atlantis' crew will conduct a final wing and nose inspection on Monday using a newly repaired inspection boom. Three station residents will depart in a Soyuz capsule on June 2, marking the beginning of the station's next crew rotation.

A 25-year-old Kentucky man, Michael Kerr, is banned from flying as he awaits trial after attacking flight crew on a Charlotte-bound plane, a judge ruled. The incident occurred on a July 21 American Airlines flight from Lexington to Charlotte, where Kerr, having consumed three Jack Daniel's, refused to sit down as the plane taxied to the gate. He threatened to break a flight attendant’s jaw and shoved her to the floor. The pilot subdued him, and Kerr was arrested by Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police. Kerr faces charges including assault on a female, interfering with a flight crew, and communicating threats. He is currently undergoing physical therapy for injuries sustained. The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA noted an increase in such incidents, often linked to alcohol consumption.

A study analyzing data from over one million U.S. teenagers over 24 years shows no significant increase in adolescent marijuana use in states that legalized medical marijuana. The findings, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, suggest that states with medical marijuana laws already had higher teen marijuana use rates before legalization. This study, led by Dr. Deborah Hasin from Columbia University Medical Center, indicates that fears of increased teen use due to medical marijuana legalization were unfounded. The researchers also noted a slight decrease in marijuana use among the youngest students, possibly due to changing perceptions or parental vigilance. The study supports previous findings that medical marijuana laws do not lead to increased adolescent use and suggests that other factors may influence teen marijuana use.

Texas Congressman Ralph Hall, 91, the oldest serving member of Congress and a World War II veteran, was injured in a two-vehicle accident in Fannin County on Saturday. Hall was a passenger in a vehicle that collided with another car on State Highway 121 near Trenton. He was airlifted to Medical Center of Plano in serious condition but has since been upgraded to stable condition. Hall suffered a hip injury and minor cuts and bruises but is expected to make a full recovery. The accident occurred as Hall was returning from the Fannin County Fair Parade in Bonham. Hall lost a primary challenge in May to John Ratcliffe and is scheduled to leave office in January after 17 consecutive terms.

The first vice presidential debate between Republican Mike Pence and Democrat Tim Kaine began at 9 p.m. Eastern Time on October 4, 2016, at Longwood University in Farmville, Virginia. The debate, moderated by Elaine Quijano of CBS News, saw the candidates clash on issues ranging from national security to immigration. Pence defended Trump, saying he would unite the country by changing Washington, while Kaine argued that Clinton’s record showed she could unite people. The candidates also debated their running mates’ charitable foundations, with Kaine criticizing the Clinton Foundation and Pence defending the Trump Foundation. Both sides accused the other of not standing up to their respective nominees on various issues. The debate highlighted the contrasting approaches of the candidates, with Pence emphasizing Trump’s business acumen and Kaine focusing on Clinton’s experience. Despite the high stakes, the debate did not significantly alter the trajectory of the presidential race.

Martin Shkreli, convicted of securities fraud, was sentenced to seven years in prison, less than half the 15 years sought by prosecutors but more than the 18 months requested by his defense. Shkreli, known for raising the price of a life-saving drug by 5,000 percent, apologized for his actions and pleaded for mercy. He was ordered to pay a $75,000 fine and $7.3 million in forfeiture. His defense portrayed him as a misunderstood genius, while prosecutors argued he stole money for his own benefit. Shkreli's antics during the trial, including offering money for a strand of Hillary Clinton's hair, contributed to his harsher sentence.

A millionaire businessman's 17-year-old daughter was kidnapped while walking her dog, and her terrified screams were the last sounds her father heard before she was murdered. The kidnappers demanded a million euros as ransom over the phone, but the girl's body was found in an abandoned farmyard near her home after a four-day search. Two suspects, a 39-year-old unemployed man and a 61-year-old factory worker, were arrested after their DNA was found on the girl’s bicycle and their cell phones were tracked. Her parents, now in police care, wrote to the kidnappers, pledging to fulfill their demands to bring their daughter home.

Researchers have uncovered mass graves in south Texas containing the bodies of unidentified migrants, buried in garbage, shopping, and body bags. The discovery was made by anthropologists from the University of Indianapolis and Baylor University, who are working on a project to identify undocumented migrants who died while crossing the border. In one burial, bones of three bodies were inside one body bag, and multiple skulls were found in biohazard bags between coffins. The remains are believed to have been buried by a local funeral home since 2005 in the Sacred Heart Burial Park in Brooks County. The funeral home, Funeraria del Angel Howard-Williams, has been paid by county officials to handle the bodies for at least 16 years. The discovery has sparked calls for an investigation, with Senator Juan Hinojosa calling for a proper investigation and burial for the deceased. The situation highlights the humanitarian challenges of U.S. immigration policies and the treatment of unidentified migrants.

Oxford English Dictionary has officially recognized the informal use of "literally" to mean "figuratively" after years of widespread misuse. The definition was added in the September 2011 edition but went unnoticed until recently. Senior editor Fiona McPherson humorously noted, "It seems to have literally slipped under the radar." This change will bring relief to commentators and politicians who have faced ridicule for using the term incorrectly. Examples include Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg describing low-rate taxpayers as "literally living in a different galaxy" and cricketer Sir Ian Botham stating batsmen surviving appeals had been "getting away with murder, literally." The dictionary now includes both the literal and figurative meanings, acknowledging that words evolve based on how people use them.

The "Leave" campaign is gaining momentum in the UK's referendum on EU membership, with support from newspapers like The Sun and concerns from investors about economic uncertainty. Polls suggest a narrow lead for "Leave," but experts caution that the final outcome is uncertain. Prime Minister David Cameron is under pressure to keep the UK in the EU, facing challenges from his own Conservative Party and opposition Labour Party. The "Leave" campaign promises economic benefits, while the "Remain" campaign warns of economic risks. The outcome could significantly impact financial markets and the global economy, with potential corrections in U.S. stocks but also opportunities for investment. The referendum on June 23 remains a closely watched event with the potential to reshape the UK's relationship with the EU and global financial markets.

The Game of Thrones creators acknowledged an unintentional inclusion of a model of George W. Bush's impaled head in the show's first season, with HBO and the producers issuing apologies. The heads were rented in bulk, and one of them resembled the former U.S. president. Both HBO and the producers expressed regret and stated they meant no disrespect, promising to remove the model from future DVD productions.

A Seneca Falls woman, Carolyn Kesel, age 46, was arrested for Felony DWI and Felony Aggravated DWI after driving erratically in a Macedon Walmart parking lot. Kesel consumed two bottles of pure vanilla extract, with a 41% alcohol content, resulting in a blood alcohol level of 0.26%, more than three times the legal limit. She claimed to be lost and unable to find her way out of the parking lot. Kesel had a prior DWI conviction in 2006. Wayne County officials, including the Mental Health Director and Probation/Correctional Director, were surprised by the high alcohol content in vanilla extract, noting that other extracts like peppermint and orange can contain even higher levels of alcohol. The Wayne County Mental Health Department suggests that habitual alcoholics might use such extracts to mask their alcohol consumption. Local stores are now informing their cashiers about the potential issue.

The United States and Israel have announced their withdrawal from UNESCO, citing anti-Israel bias and the need for "fundamental reform" in the U.N. cultural agency. The U.S. decision, effective as of December 31, 2018, comes after the U.S. had already stopped funding UNESCO in 2011 due to the organization's admission of Palestine as a member. The U.S. now owes over $500 million in back payments. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson made the decision, stating it reflects U.S. concerns with mounting arrears, the need for reform, and continued anti-Israel bias. UNESCO Director-General Irina Bokova expressed disappointment, calling it a loss for the United Nations family and multilateralism. The U.S. will maintain its presence as an observer state. The move is seen as a further estrangement from an organization that the U.S. helped establish after World War II.

A 7-year-old boy named Yamato Tanooka was found alive and unharmed in a military hut after being left in a forest in Hokkaido, Japan, as punishment by his parents. Yamato, who was reportedly without food or water, was discovered by military personnel 5 kilometers from where he was last seen. His father, Takayuki Tanooka, expressed regret for the incident, saying, "I feel very sorry for the boy as I came down on him hard." Yamato's ordeal sparked a debate about parental discipline in Japan, where the culture traditionally views children as family property. The search involved over 180 rescuers, including military personnel, who combed the area after the boy's parents initially misled police about his whereabouts. Yamato was found to be in good health except for mild dehydration and minor scratches.

Elderly South Koreans gathered in North Korea for a six-day family reunion, marking the first such event in three years and a rare show of cooperation between the two Koreas. Around 100 South Koreans, selected by lottery from over 70,000 applicants, traveled to North Korea’s Mount Kumgang resort to reunite with relatives they hadn’t seen in six decades. The emotional reunions, which began on Thursday, included meetings between siblings, parents, and children, with some participants arriving in wheelchairs or on stretchers due to their advanced age. The event, despite its brevity, symbolizes a shared interest in reconnecting long-lost relatives, despite the ongoing division on the Korean Peninsula. The South Korean government hopes these reunions will lead to broader improvements in inter-Korean relations, though many participants are likely to be among the last to see their relatives due to their advanced age.

A man accused of kidnapping and torturing his wife while under home confinement on charges of beating and abducting her was declared brain dead after a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Kevin Ewing, 47, was found alive in a barn with a gunshot wound but was later pronounced brain dead at a hospital. His wife, Tierne Ewing, 48, was found dead in the same barn with a gunshot wound to the head. Kevin Ewing had previously been accused of holding Tierne hostage for 12 days, during which he allegedly beat and burned her. Despite a protection-from-abuse order and an arrest warrant, Kevin Ewing was released on $100,000 bail. The assistant district attorney fought to keep him in jail but was unsuccessful. Kevin Ewing was suspected of removing his electronic monitoring bracelet before abducting Tierne. The case highlights concerns about the effectiveness of electronic monitoring systems in preventing such incidents.

2011 is off to a rocky start for the Favre family. Brett Favre, the future Hall of Fame quarterback, is facing a sexual harassment lawsuit and a possible lawsuit from a broadcaster. Meanwhile, his younger sister, Brandi Favre, has been arrested for a methamphetamine-related charge in a raid on a suspected meth lab in Mississippi. The incident occurred just a few miles from where Brett and his siblings grew up. Brandi has a history of legal troubles, including a drive-by shooting and shoplifting incident. As the Favre family faces these challenges, the focus remains on Brett's career and personal life.

Rowan County Clerk Kim Davis has asked a federal judge to not hold her in contempt of court for refusing to issue marriage licenses. Davis argues that the order "irreparably and irreversibly violates her conscience" as it directs her to authorize and issue same-sex marriage licenses bearing her name and approval. She has been refusing to give anyone a marriage license since the U.S. Supreme Court legalized same-sex marriage, citing her religious objections. The contempt hearing is scheduled for Thursday. Davis's attorneys argue that the order affects her religious beliefs and that she should not be punished yet as she still has an appeal pending. Meanwhile, local and state legislators are considering legislative responses, including removing clerks' names from marriage license paperwork or transferring the authority to a state agency, though lawmakers are not scheduled to convene until January.

Qatar Airways CEO Akbar al-Baker faced criticism after stating that his position requires a male leader due to its challenges. Al-Baker later issued an apology, emphasizing Qatar Airways' commitment to gender equality and highlighting the airline's record of employing women in various leadership roles. His comments drew backlash and groans from the audience at the International Air Transport Association's annual conference in Sydney. Al-Baker clarified that his statement was made in jest and not reflective of his true beliefs. He also expressed a willingness to support a female CEO candidate for the airline.

The mother of a 22-month-old toddler who died after being left in a hot SUV has been under scrutiny following her husband's murder charges. Leanna Harris, a 30-year-old dietitian, told police she researched how children die in hot cars, describing it as her "worst fear." On the day of her son Cooper's death, she acted strangely when informed her son had not been dropped off at daycare, calmly stating her husband must have left him in the car. During a probable cause hearing, she asked her husband, "Did you say too much?" Leanna Harris has maintained her loyalty to her husband, Ross, stating he was a "wonderful father" and expressing no anger toward him. However, her stoic demeanor and public statements have raised questions about her potential involvement. The case has sparked debate about the role of the mother in such tragic incidents, with some questioning whether she should be considered a witness or suspect.

During an AFC Champions League match between Iran's Sepahan and Saudi Arabia's Al-Ahli, Sepahan midfielder Adel Kolahkaj found himself in a shocking situation when he picked up a piece of trash from the field and threw it. What he didn't expect was that the object he threw was actually an explosive device that detonated upon impact. The incident highlights the unexpected and dangerous situations players can face during a game, with Kolahkaj emerging as extremely lucky to have survived the explosion.
Grateful for President Trump, Jared Kushner, and those who contributed to Ms. Alice Marie Johnson's commutation, which offers hope to many others deserving a second chance.

A parolee suspected of cutting off his ankle monitor and carrying out a series of killings in the Houston area has been arrested and charged with capital murder. Jose Gilberto Rodriguez, 46, is accused of at least three fatal shootings and two other violent robberies in the past week. Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez announced the arrest, describing Rodriguez as a "possible serial killer." Rodriguez, a high-risk registered sex offender, was released from prison in September 2017 after serving part of a 20-year sentence for attempted aggravated sexual assault. The killings targeted random victims, including an elderly couple and a METROLift bus driver. Rodriguez is expected to face three capital murder charges, with authorities promising increased efforts to monitor and apprehend parolees.

Washington, D.C., is undertaking a three-year, $1.5 million project to estimate the city’s entire cat population, both feral and pet cats, through the D.C. Cat Count. The initiative involves collaboration between the Humane Rescue Alliance, the Humane Society of the United States, the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute, and PetSmart Charities. Using camera traps, household surveys, and an analysis of shelter populations, the project aims to better understand and manage the city’s cat population. The effort is seen as crucial for improving programs to spay and neuter stray cats and facilitate cat adoptions. While cats are often blamed for wildlife predation, the project also recognizes their potential in pest control. The D.C. Cat Count hopes to provide data that can help tailor programs and services to the needs of the city’s feline residents.

A 24-year-old woman named Laura, suffering from depression since childhood, has been granted the right to die in Belgium, where euthanasia is legal for those with "unbearable physical or mental suffering." Laura, who entered a psychiatric facility at 21, told local media she feels life is not worth living and plans to end her life, while also arranging her funeral and final words to her mother and grandmother. She attributes her desire to die to both her upbringing and her own persistent mental health issues. The case highlights a growing trend of younger individuals seeking euthanasia in Belgium, where the law was expanded in 2013 to include terminally ill children.

The University of Phoenix Stadium has a history of giving the New England Patriots unfortunate moments in Super Bowl play. In Super Bowl XLIX, Seattle Seahawks receiver Jermaine Kearse made a catch that may have been even more unbelievable than David Tyree's famous helmet catch. With the Seahawks looking to score the go-ahead touchdown late in the fourth quarter, New England cornerback Malcolm Butler attempted to break up a deep pass from Seattle quarterback Russell Wilson to Kearse. However, the ball took a couple of bounces and stayed up long enough for Kearse to make the catch while lying on the ground. Unfortunately for the Seahawks, Wilson threw an interception a couple of plays later, essentially ending the game with a 28-24 score. After scoring the touchdown, Seattle Seahawks wide receiver Doug Baldwin performed an unusual celebration by pretending to defecate on the football, which cost him a 15-yard penalty. Passengers and crew foiled a hijacking attempt by six people on a plane in China's restive Xinjiang region. The incident occurred just after takeoff from Hotan for the regional capital of Urumqi, and the plane returned safely with the suspects detained, according to a regional airline and state media. The Tianshan regional government's news portal reported that the hijackers tried to break into the cockpit with a broken crutch but were overpowered. At least seven passengers and crew were injured. The government stated that the suspects were men from the Uighur minority group, but no details were available on their motives or identities, and police were still investigating. Hotan has been the scene of recent clashes between ethnic Uighurs and authorities, who say they face an organized terrorist threat from radical Muslim groups in the region.

ABC's shows will be available on Apple's iPad through a new app, allowing viewers to watch free, ad-supported episodes from 20 ABC shows via Wi-Fi. Users can also purchase episodes via iTunes. Bob Iger, CEO of Walt Disney, sees the iPad as a compelling consumer device for original, interactive content. This announcement follows ABC's recent episode of "Modern Family" featuring the iPad prominently.

Groupon is reportedly about to close a $950 million funding round that could value the company between $4 billion and $8 billion, according to VCExperts. This move is aimed at Groupon's goal of world domination, involving potential rapid acquisitions of rival group-buying shops, increased local sales force presence, and significant technology investments. While the funding will partly be used to cash out existing investors, the bulk will support Groupon's ambitions to solidify its market position and transform e-commerce.

Longtime conservative columnist George Will has left the Republican Party and is urging others to ensure Donald Trump does not win the nomination. Will told PJ Media that he has changed his voter registration to "unaffiliated" and stated, "Make sure he loses. Grit their teeth for four years and win the White House." His decision comes after House Speaker Paul Ryan endorsed Trump. Will has previously criticized Trump, predicting he would be the "most unpopular nominee ever" and unable to garner support from women, minorities, and young voters.

A shooting at Toronto's Eaton Centre mall left one man dead and seven others injured, including a 13-year-old boy in critical condition. Gunfire erupted around 6:30 p.m. in the food court, with multiple victims suffering gunshot wounds and injuries from trampling. Police believe a lone shooter is responsible and are reviewing mall camera footage and interviewing witnesses. Mayor Rob Ford and police chief Bill Blair expressed their condolences and commitment to apprehending the suspect. The incident left the mall evacuated and closed for the day, with many shoppers and employees recounting chaotic scenes of panic and confusion.

TV One's new docudrama series, "Find Our Missing," aims to address the underrepresentation of missing persons of color in mainstream media. The series, hosted by "Law & Order" alum S. Epatha Merkerson, focuses on two cases in each hourlong episode, drawing attention to the disproportionate number of missing African-Americans. Statistics show that blacks make up nearly a third of the nation’s missing-person cases, despite comprising only 12% of the total population. The series hopes to encourage viewers to come forward with information, emphasizing the personal impact of missing persons on their families and communities. The premiere episode features the case of Pamela Butler, a 47-year-old federal employee who vanished from her home in Washington, D.C., and the disappearance of a 5-year-old boy, Hasanni Campbell, in Oakland, California. The show's approach is quiet and empathetic, aiming to humanize the issue rather than sensationalize it.

Portland police arrested over 50 protesters as they cleared Occupy Portland encampments, part of a nationwide trend of authorities dismantling similar protests. Demonstrators, some in gas masks, clashed with riot police in a tense standoff that lasted into the evening. Mayor Sam Adams cited health and safety issues, while protesters called for a peaceful resolution. Simultaneously, other cities faced similar challenges: Salt Lake City dismantled a camp, Oakland issued eviction notices, and Philadelphia beefed up police patrols. The movement, which began in New York, faces growing pressure from authorities and changing dynamics as protesters seek new strategies.

The 60 Minutes interview with Stormy Daniels, who alleges she had an affair with President Trump in 2006 and 2007, will air on Sunday, March 25 at 7 p.m. ET/PT on CBS. Daniels will speak to Anderson Cooper about the relationship for the first and only television interview on the topic. The interview comes as Daniels faces legal challenges, including a suit against Trump to invalidate a non-disclosure agreement, and as she prepares to return the $130,000 payment she received. The segment will also examine the potential legal and political ramifications of the payment made by Trump's attorney, Michael Cohen. Daniels' background in adult entertainment and her recent political foray add layers to the story, potentially impacting the broader narrative of sexual misconduct allegations against the president.

Egypt's public prosecutor has summoned former President Hosni Mubarak and his sons Gamal and Alaa for questioning in investigations related to the killing of protesters and embezzlement of public funds. Mubarak, who was ousted after 18 days of protests, denied wrongdoing in a pre-recorded message aired on Al Arabiya television, stating he would cooperate with the prosecutor and defend himself against "unjust campaign" claims. The move has drawn criticism from protesters who demand immediate arrest of Mubarak. Meanwhile, security forces used live ammunition, tear gas, and rubber bullets to disperse protesters in Tahrir Square, resulting in at least two deaths and dozens wounded. Protest leaders issued statements aimed at de-escalating tensions, while the military denied any involvement and accused protesters of being infiltrated by "thugs."

A deceased woman, Martha Kunkle, whose name appeared on thousands of affidavits used by a major debt collector, has resurfaced as a case study in the inaccuracies and potential fraud within the debt-collection industry. Kunkle's name was used by employees who worked with her daughter, leading to lawsuits filed against borrowers. The issue came to light in 2008 when a Montana resident sued Portfolio Recovery Associates, one of the nation's largest debt collectors, for using Kunkle's name in affidavits. The company acknowledged the mistake and stopped using Kunkle's name in documents. However, the case highlights the broader problem of mass-produced, sloppy, and inaccurate documentation in debt collection. Regulators and judges are increasingly scrutinizing the practices of debt collectors, with some calling for more disclosure and accountability.

Police in Tucson are in disagreement with a small Indiana town over the ownership of a Tommy gun taken from notorious gangster John Dillinger during his arrest in 1934. Peru, Indiana, claims the gun was stolen from their police department in 1933 by Dillinger's accomplice posing as an insurance agent. Tucson officials argue it is an important part of their city's history and are hesitant to return the weapon. The origin of the gun is unclear, making it difficult to determine its rightful ownership. Peru officials believe the serial number can prove their claim.

Arkansas fired football coach Bobby Petrino on Tuesday for misleading the university about his relationship with his mistress, Jessica Dorrell, and hiring her to a key position. Athletic director Jeff Long announced the termination, citing Petrino's "pattern of misleading and manipulative behavior." Petrino, 51, had maintained an inappropriate relationship with Dorrell, a 25-year-old employee, for a significant period and had given her $20,000. Petrino's hiring of Dorrell as student-athlete development coordinator was seen as a conflict of interest. Petrino, who built Arkansas into a football powerhouse, was fired "with cause," meaning he will not receive the $18 million buyout stipulated in his contract. Petrino issued a lengthy apology, focusing on the damage he had done to his family.

A man in Madison County, Illinois, is suing Pepsi over finding a mouse in his Mountain Dew. The plaintiff, Ronald Ball, claims he bought a can from a vending machine at work, drank it, and then vomited. He found a mouse in the can when he poured the soda into a Styrofoam cup. Pepsi's defense? The mouse would have dissolved in the soda before Ball could have consumed it. The company argues that by the time Ball noticed the mouse, it had turned into a "jelly-like" substance, making the lawsuit essentially baseless. The case highlights an unusual legal battle over a potentially hazardous but perhaps undetectable ingredient in a soft drink.

An Australian man named Gable Tostee, 30, was acquitted of murdering a New Zealand woman, Warriena Wright, during their first Tinder date. Wright, 26, fell to her death from Tostee's balcony on the Gold Coast in August 2014. Prosecutors argued she tried to escape but fell, while Tostee's defense highlighted a 199-minute audio recording on his phone showing his alleged threats and her pleas for release. After four days of deliberation, the jury found Tostee not guilty of murder and manslaughter. Tostee expressed relief, hoping to move on with his life. The audio recording played a crucial role in the trial, capturing intense moments of confrontation and Tostee's alleged threats.

Oscar Pistorius' lawyer, Barry Roux, argued that Pistorius, feeling vulnerable and anxious due to his disability, snapped like an abused woman the night he killed his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp, during closing arguments. Roux portrayed Pistorius as a vulnerable man, insecure due to his condition, and claimed he accidentally shot through a bathroom door, mistaking it for an intruder. The defense acknowledged Pistorius' past argumentative behavior but maintained he did not intentionally kill Steenkamp. Judge Thokozile Masipa questioned the "slow burn" comparison, asking how it applied to Pistorius. The trial, which began in March, is set to conclude today, with Judge Masipa expected to announce a verdict soon.

Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton secured a decisive victory in South Carolina's primary, winning 74% of the vote compared to Bernie Sanders' 26%, buoyed by strong support from black voters who favored her over Barack Obama in 2008. Clinton's win, following her narrow victory in Nevada, strengthens her position as the frontrunner heading into Super Tuesday. Clinton emphasized unity and economic issues, while Sanders focused on economic inequality and campaign finance reform. The outcome underscores Clinton's appeal to moderate and conservative Democrats, as well as older voters. Both candidates campaigned in Super Tuesday states, with Clinton focusing on key Southern states, while Sanders targeted Midwest and Northeast states. The race remains competitive, with Sanders hoping to win several states on Super Tuesday to maintain a delegate lead.

A stampede during New Year's Eve celebrations in Shanghai's Bund area killed at least 36 people and injured 47. President Xi Jinping demanded an investigation into the incident, which occurred in Chenyi Square and was triggered by large crowds exceeding predictions. Shanghai police regretted their insufficient intervention and acknowledged fewer officers were deployed than usual. The cause of the crush remains under investigation, with some reports suggesting fake money thrown from a building triggered the chaos. President Xi instructed local authorities to ensure safety during upcoming festivals and to provide prompt treatment for the injured.

Saturday Night Live began their latest episode with a message of support to Paris after Friday’s attacks, skipping their usual cold open. "Paris is the city of light, and here in New York City, we know that light will never go out," Cecily Strong told the audience. "Our love and support is with everyone there tonight. We stand with you." Strong then repeated the message in French. Elizabeth Banks hosted the show, with music provided by Disclosure featuring guest spots from Sam Smith and Lorde.

Actor Bryan Cranston hinted during a CNN interview that a potential comeback for his iconic character Walter White on "Breaking Bad" is not entirely ruled out. When asked about Walter's apparent death in the series finale, Cranston playfully responded, "You never saw bags zip up or anyone say... you know," leaving the door open for a possible resurrection. The original series concluded in 2013, but a spinoff "Better Call Saul" is currently in development, with creator Vince Gilligan suggesting some "Breaking Bad" characters might appear in the new show.

Apple's recent iOS 5.0.1 update aimed to fix a battery drain issue but has reportedly failed to do so for some users. Early adopters on Apple's Support Forums report that their battery life remains poor, with some even experiencing faster battery depletion than before the update. While a minority of users claim the update helped, many continue to face significant battery drain problems, raising questions about the effectiveness of the fix. Apple stated that the update addressed many battery issues but acknowledged some remaining problems. Users are advised to perform a full discharge and recharge or reset their devices to potentially resolve the issue.

Police have made a breakthrough in the 47-year-old case of the abduction of three-year-old Cheryl Grimmer from a Wollongong beach. Detectives believe a teenager, now in his 60s, may be the suspect after finding information missed in the original investigation. The family, including Cheryl's brothers, is urging the suspect to come forward for closure. Cheryl's parents died without knowing what happened to their daughter. Detectives are offering a $100,000 reward for information leading to an arrest. The case remains unsolved, with no trace of Cheryl found despite extensive searches.

A Texas high school cheerleader who was dismissed from her squad for refusing to cheer for a basketball player accused of sexually assaulting her lost her appeal at the U.S. Supreme Court. The Supreme Court declined to hear the case without comment, upholding a federal appeals court ruling that the cheerleader, identified as H.S., was speaking for the school and had no right to remain silent when called on to cheer the athlete by name. H.S., 16 at the time, claimed she was raped by the player at a party in 2008, but a state grand jury declined to indict. Despite the player's return to the team, H.S. refused to cheer for him during a 2009 game, leading to her dismissal. The family sued the school district, alleging violations of free speech and equal protection, but the courts ruled against them, stating that as a cheerleader, H.S. served as a "mouthpiece" for the school.

French scientists have developed an artificial heart that can beat for up to five years, potentially solving the chronic shortage of donor hearts for transplant surgery. The device, created by the biomedical firm Carmat, was implanted in a 75-year-old Frenchman during a 10-hour operation. Unlike previous artificial hearts, this model is fully artificial and self-regulating, mimicking the functions of a real heart with electrical sensors and microprocessors. The patient, described as "near death" with no other options, is reportedly responding well. The artificial heart, weighing 900g and powered by external batteries, is designed to reduce rejection by the host and improve the quality of life for patients. It is expected to cost around £100,000 to £135,000, comparable to the overall cost of a donor heart transplant. The device, which can fit 86% of men and 20% of women, is currently under clinical trials
